title: Chartstopper: September 11, 2026
author: Michael Normyle
description: Between rising oil prices and this week’s inflation data, markets are increasingly certain the Federal Reserve will hike rates next week.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Core CPI accelerates, boosting rate hike odds Oil surges to $100 as Iran conflict escalates Markets price in 85%+ chance of Fed hike next week Treasury buyback disappoints, lifting yields Nasdaq-100® finishes flat amid rate pressure This Week Between rising oil prices and this week’s inflation data, markets are increasingly certain the Federal Reserve will hike rates next week. A big reason is that today’s CPI report showed core CPI accelerating in August , rising 0.3% month-on-month, boosted in part by wireless phone services, airfares, and hotels. That was a bigger gain than markets expected (0.2%), and while the Fed’s target is headline (PCE) inflation, the Fed often prefers core inflation as a better guide to inflation trends. Another reason is that U.S. oil prices rose nearly $10 this week to $100 per barrel – putting it around its high since May. This comes as the Iran conflict intensifies, with attacks prompting Saudi Arabia to close energy facilities and shut down its East-West oil pipeline that can carry 7 million barrels per day. The U.S. struck five Iranian oil tankers , resulting in Iranian retaliation . There have also been reports that Iran will escalate its counterattacks and that President Trump has been briefed that the conflict could last through the end of his term . So, markets now see a greater than 85% chance that the Fed hikes rates next week, compared to just 50% before last week’s strong jobs report. That wasn’t all for rates drama this week, though. Ten-year Treasury yields rose after the Treasury Department announced it was buying back $6 billion in bonds – below expectations for up to $10 billion in buybacks. As a result, 10-year Treasury yields are up nearly 20 basis points this week to almost 5% – near a three-year high. And higher rates weighed on stocks, leaving the Nasdaq-100® down 1% for the week. title: Does Order Protection Matter? Data Says Yes!
author: Phil Mackintosh
description: Explore the implications of the Order Protection Rule, and what eliminations might mean for spreads and the NBBO.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways OPR Under Review: Mixed feedback on SEC proposal to eliminate the Order Protection Rule. Natural Experiment: Round lot changes offering real-world data on protected vs. unprotected quotes. Protection Tightens Spreads: Immediate narrowing on gaining NBBO protection; widening on losing it. Consistent Across Stocks: 81% improved when protected, ~90% dis-improved when unprotected — not rebate-driven. Real Costs at Stake: Higher trading costs, lower valuations, higher cost of capital — repeal should be paired Best-Ex, access fee cap, and SIP reforms. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has proposed eliminating the Order Protection Rule (OPR) . Comments on the proposed rule change are in, and there is far from overwhelming agreement or support. Today, we look at what the implications of OPR are, and what eliminations might mean for spreads and the NBBO. What we find is that order protection significantly lowers spread. In short, OPR probably matters to investors . We use the new changes to round lots to compare how much NBBO matters One problem with estimating whether OPR matters is finding data on what happened when it previously didn’t, and when it did (with all other things being the same). Luckily, the SEC’s recent round lot changes give us that data. However, in contrast to what we did here , this time, we use the fact that odd lots have always been on the tape (as the chart below shows). Chart 1: New dynamic round lots change the value required to set the NBBO, but lit odd lots still exist inside the spread What happens to odd lot spreads when they become protected? There have always been 10-lot BBO spreads and 40-lot BBO spreads. It’s just that, in the past, they were not protected. If we calculate the 40-lot spread before and after it was an NBBO (using stocks that switched round lot), we see that: When it became protected, the 40-share spreads fell. When stocks went back the other way (which some already have), the 40-share spreads widened. Not surprisingly, the same thing happened for stocks put into the 10-share round lot group. What was surprising was how much the 10-share spread improved! Chart 2: Order protection narrows the spread Gaining protection tightens spreads, losing it widens spread Looking at these spread changes over time, we see that the 40-share spread changes almost immediately when it becomes a protected (round) lot — and it widens when the opposite happens. Chart 3: Odd lot spreads shift immediately as new round lot takes effect This is a relatively new rule, so the sample size is small, especially for May changes (line thickness shows the number of stocks). For example, there are: 284 stocks that moved from a 100-share round lot to a 40-share round lot. 39 stocks that moved from 40 to 100-share round lot. 5 stocks that moved from 40 to 10-share round lot. 12 stocks that moved from 100 to 10-share round lot. But importantly, the stock-by-stock data also shows that the spread improvements (or dis-improvements when increasing the round lot) were consistent across almost all stocks (Chart 4): 81% of all green dots (40-share spread as they became NBBO) improved. 89.7% of all pink dots (40-share spread as they lost NBBO) dis-improved. We even see consistent results for 10-share spreads and stocks moving to the 10-share NBBO (blue dots). Chart 4: The round lot effect is consistent across most stocks So, the outcome here is clear. OPR matters to spreads and depth! And it’s not because of rebates (they’re paid on all liquidity provision). Wider spreads have real costs to companies and investors This matters because wider spreads hurt investors by adding to trade costs (even those trading off-exchange ) and companies by reducing valuations and raising costs of capital — one of the important things that we learned from the tick size pilot . The mechanism is different here, but the lesson is the same: Wider spreads aren't free. That’s why it’s important, if the SEC ultimately decides to adopt its proposal to rescind the Order Protection Rule, it also must reform other aspects of market structure — like Best-Ex rules, the access fee cap, and the SIP incentives at the same time — to ensure that the net effects of the SEC’s reforms will be positive for investors and the markets.

title: Governance, Clarity, and the Next Phase of Capital Formation: Texas Leads the Way
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: While Texas's rise as an economic power is often told as a story of population growth and corporate relocations, what increasingly sets the state apart is something less visible but more durable: a governance and regulatory framework.
content: Capital follows rules. Not regulations in the bureaucratic sense but clarity. The kind of structural predictability that allows a board to act with conviction, an investor to model risk with confidence, and a company to plan in decades rather than quarters. That distinction matters now more than ever. Because while Texas's rise as an economic power is often told as a story of population growth and corporate relocations, what increasingly sets the state apart is something less visible but more durable: a governance and regulatory framework designed to eliminate ambiguity, which only creates unnecessary risk. "Texas takes a simple proposition of the importance of legal clarity and builds on it," says Ed Knight, Executive Vice Chairman of Nasdaq and Chairman of the Nasdaq Texas Advisory Board. " Texas is saying we do not want to force you to go to court. Here are the rules. We're going to make them as clear as possible, and we're going to do it in a way that doesn't encourage needless litigation." That confidence in clarity is beginning to reshape how companies evaluate not just where to operate but where to incorporate, where to resolve disputes, and how to align with capital markets . Jurisdiction is becoming a strategic decision. Remember: at one time New Jersey was the state where companies incorporated and then Delaware presented a different proposition. Now Texas is stepping up with a better idea. Codifying Predictability: The Role of SB 29 At the center of this evolution is Texas Senate Bill 29, signed into law in May 2025. It represents one of the most consequential updates to the Texas Business Organizations Code in decades, and its aim is deceptively simple: bring greater clarity to corporate governance and reduce ambiguity in disputes between boards, shareholders, and stakeholders. This benefits all corporate stakeholders not just boards. "Most executives — CEOs, general counsels, CFOs — all they want is certainty: tell me what the rules are," Knight explains. "Tell me where the safe harbor is. I'm going to comply. I don't want to challenge the law. In fact, with the cost of litigation today and the risk associated with it, companies want to avoid the courtroom and rationally manage that risk." The practical implications are meaningful. SB 29 codifies the business judgment rule, establishing a statutory presumption under clear conditions that directors and officers act in good faith, on an informed basis, and in the best interests of the company. To challenge board decisions, plaintiffs must now meet a more rational threshold and demonstrate fraud, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law, supported by specific and well-pleaded facts. This is a clearer standard than exists in Delaware, where courts have discretion to apply additional standards beyond the business judgment rule depending on the facts and allegations of a given case. SB 29 also introduces a set of governance tools that allow companies to define how they operate: The ability to establish minimum ownership thresholds (up to 3%) for shareholder derivative actions, reducing exposure to low merit claims. Flexibility to define dispute processes in governing documents, including jury trial waivers and forum selection. Expanded latitude for alternative entities to modify or eliminate fiduciary duties contractually. These provisions shift governance toward a framework where expectations are set clearly at formation. That clarity can shape how capital is allocated, how boards make decisions, and how investors evaluate risk. The Delaware Contrast Knight, who served as Nasdaq's General Counsel before becoming Executive Vice Chairman, frames the competitive dynamic directly: "If you go to Delaware, what they would tell you is, ‘We have great lawyers and judges.’ Well, my board doesn't really like litigation. So, I don't want to get in front of your judges or frankly hire any of your lawyers." The problem, he argues, is structural. Delaware's rules are "very dense and hard to apply and often result in shareholder litigation." The consequence: a company could execute a transaction — complete the process, satisfy its board, close the deal — and still face litigation after the fact over the composition of a special committee or some technical procedural question. "Owning six shares of stock and then tying a company up in court and creating the risk of an award of hundreds of millions of dollars in damages — that's not rational and represents a misapplication of risk and capital," Knight says. "Texas is bringing some common sense to the rules in this area." Texas has done something Delaware never did: it created an advance judicial ruling mechanism. When a board forms a special committee to oversee a transaction, it can now go to the Texas Business Court in advance and ask: is this committee properly constituted? The ruling eliminates the post-close litigation trap that has defined M&A practice in Delaware for decades. "You have transparency and certainty," Knight says. "And I think the fact that Exxon — which is led by some of the best business executives in the world and advised by a great legal team— would not have made the move to incorporate in Texas unless it was in the interest of its shareholders and represented good legal public policy. I know they care deeply about their shareholders." SB 1057 and the Mechanics of Governance While SB 29 establishes the foundation, Texas Senate Bill 1057 builds on it by addressing how governance operates in practice, particularly around shareholder proposals. It restores common sense to the proxy proposal process. Under SB 1057, companies incorporated in Texas that are also headquartered in the state or listed on a Texas-based exchange can modify their governing documents so that only shareholders holding at least $1 million in market value or 3% of voting shares may submit proposals. That threshold is significantly higher than the SEC's current rule, which requires a combination of market value and holding duration, allowing a shareholder owning as little as $2,000 in market value held for at least 3 years, to place a matter on the proxy. The legislation also requires that shareholders actively solicit other shareholders representing at least 67% of the voting power entitled to vote on a proposal or it can be excluded. The combined effect is cumulative. Together, SB 29 and SB 1057 create a governance model where statutory standards and internal processes are more closely aligned — giving companies greater control over the conduct of their corporate affairs. The Proxy Advisory Problem Among the most consequential (and least understood) governance issues facing public companies is the role of proxy advisory firms. And it is here that Nasdaq's track record becomes most relevant to the Texas story. Proxy advisory firms (such as ISS and Glass Lewis) issue voting recommendations that can influence key corporate matters, yet they are not subject to the same regulatory requirements as stock exchanges, broker-dealers, or public companies. "Stock exchanges — regulated. Broker-dealers — regulated. Public companies — regulated. The people who do the underwriting — regulated. The people who do the credit evaluation — regulated," says Terry Campbell, Senior Vice President of Governmental Affairs at Nasdaq. "The only participant in our ecosystem that's not regulated is the proxy advisors. And they control in some cases 30 to 40 percent of the votes." For more than a decade, Nasdaq has expressed concern with the lack of meaningful regulation governing proxy advisory firms and advocated for greater transparency, including requiring proxy advisors to disclose their methodologies, open their processes to public comment, and be subject to oversight comparable to other market participants. In 2013, Ed Knight wrote a Wall Street Journal op-ed calling out the lack of transparency in the proxy advisory model — one of the first times a public company executive had publicly challenged the system. "We had companies that, when there were mistakes on their proxy voting recommendations, would call the proxy advisors, and the proxy advisors would say: if you're not an S&P 500 company, we don't talk to you," Campbell explains. "We won't even respond. We won't even take your call." The issue is one of influence and of process. When a public company wants to change a corporate governance standard, it must file with the SEC, open a public comment period, respond to every letter, and receive a formal vote. Proxy advisory firms face none of those requirements. "The incongruity of it makes no sense," Campbell says. "What we're talking about is frankly transparency, what they're doing and how they come up with their conclusions, and allowing the public to participate." Texas has now moved where Washington has stalled. The state has the sovereign authority under the Constitution to pass laws regulating these firms at the state level, and Nasdaq intends to bring a comprehensive agenda to the Texas legislature. A Supporting Layer: Business Courts and Legal Infrastructure Alongside these statutory changes, Texas has introduced a dedicated forum for resolving complex business disputes. The Texas Business Court (TBC), established in 2023 and operational since 2024, was designed to handle corporate governance matters, commercial contracts, and other high-stakes business litigation. Subsequent legislation has expanded its jurisdiction and lowered thresholds for eligible cases, increasing accessibility for a broader range of companies. Early TBC decisions have generally emphasized contract clarity and adherence to governing documents reinforcing the direction set by recent legislative reforms. Where Governance and Market Access Converge For companies, decisions around incorporation and governance are increasingly connected to how they access capital markets, and Nasdaq Texas was built at that intersection. Launched in 2026, Nasdaq Texas extends Nasdaq's platform into the state, giving companies a capital markets presence in Texas backed by the same global liquidity, investor base, and market infrastructure that have always defined Nasdaq. That reach recently expanded further. Nasdaq Texas was approved by the Texas State Securities Board as a recognized and responsible stock exchange, a designation that exempts securities fully listed on Nasdaq Texas from separate Texas state securities registration, regardless of whether the listing company is incorporated or headquartered in Texas. This is a distinct benefit from Texas's governance framework under SB 29 and SB 1057, which applies based on a company's state of incorporation, not where its securities are listed. Companies that are Texas-incorporated can draw on that statutory governance clarity, while any company (Texas-domiciled or not) that lists on Nasdaq Texas gains the added advantage of streamlined state securities compliance. Together, these create a compelling proposition: for Texas-incorporated companies, alignment with a growing economic and legal center, paired with a reduced regulatory burden; and for all listed companies, the backing of Nasdaq's technology and global market structure. A Framework Still Evolving The impact of SB 29 and SB 1057 will continue to take shape as companies adopt these tools and as legal interpretation evolves. The Business Court will build precedent over time, further clarifying how the statutes are applied in practice. That ongoing development is part of what makes this moment meaningful. Texas is increasingly positioned to support modern capital formation through governance clarity, legal infrastructure, and market access working in concert — and Nasdaq Texas's expanded platform only reinforces that trajectory. "Capital flows where the rules are understood," Knight says. "These markets are evolving, and what the markets need today won't be the same thing they need in five years. We're trying to stay ahead of that." © 2026 Nasdaq, Inc. title: Index Monthly Scorecard: August 2026
author: Nasdaq Index Insights Team
description: Softer inflation and economic data initially reduced September Fed hike expectations, but hawkish Fed comments revived rate hike odds. Rising Treasury yields and strong Q2 earnings supported equities, with gains broadening beyond mega-cap tech to banks and small caps.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Nasdaq Monthly Index Performance Commentary – August 2026 •    The Nasdaq-100 Index® (NDX®) rebounded in August 2026 to finish higher by 4.2%. •    As Q2 2026 earnings wind down, 85 out of 102 Nasdaq-100® companies representing 85% of the index by weight beat EPS expectations by an average of 11.2% with an index level growth rate of 78% as of August 31st. •    The broadening of equity returns occurred against the backdrop of a strong earnings season and generally resilient U.S. economic data. •    Nasdaq’s suite of indexes ended August with 106 out of 130 indexes tracked in our report posting gains and the average index up 5%. Chart of the Month Source: Bloomberg.  Data as of August 31, 2026. Executive Summary Softer Tier 1 U.S. economic data—July NFPs and retail sales—coupled with cooler-than-expected inflation—July CPI (core inflation was up just 2.5% year-over-year in July, the slowest since 2021), PPI, and PCE—had initially caused markets to largely price out a September Fed rate. However, following Fed Chair Warsh’s hawkish-tilting speech at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium at the end of August, the markets are back to pricing in a 65% chance of a hike in September and at least one rate hike by year’s end, according to Bloomberg. Markets have concurrently been focused on elevated Treasury yields on account of still sticky inflation given higher oil prices, a broadly resilient U.S. economy, lingering Fed policy uncertainties, and ongoing U.S. government fiscal concerns. This culminated in the Treasury announcing on August 19th that it will double the level of government debt buybacks in the next few months, to “at least” $4 billion, targeting the sensitive longer-duration segment of the market, according to Bloomberg. 10-year yields are now higher by around 10 basis points from when Secretary Bessent announced these measures and approaching 4.80%—highest since January 2025, according to Bloomberg. A strong Q2 earnings season, coupled with the aforementioned initial tamping down of Fed rate hike angst, helped equities rebound in August. A developing theme since the June 2nd Nasdaq-100 highs has been the broadening of equity returns, as shown in the above Chart of the Month. While the PHLX Semiconductor Index rebounded slightly in August (+2%) after its largest monthly decline since December 2002 (-20.6% in July), the more cyclically and domestically geared areas of banks and small caps have outperformed since early June. In fact, the Nasdaq U.S. Small Cap Index (NQUSS) had its strongest year-to-date return through August—up by 17.7%— in the last 5 years (+26.3%). The relative performance of small-cap and cyclical indexes was consistent with broader market participation beyond mega-cap technology companies. Nasdaq Indexes August 2026 Performance Recap Among the 130 indexes tracked in this report, 106 finished August in positive territory, while 24 ended with negative returns. The best-performing index was the PHLX Gold/Silver Sector™ Index (XAU™) , delivering a return of 32.4%. The weakest performance was from the Dorsey Wright Industrials Tech Leaders™ Index (DWIDX™) , which declined 8.3% for the month. The average return across all 130 indexes was 5.0%. Nasdaq Featured Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. Thirteen out of fifteen Nasdaq Featured Indexes registered positive returns in August as the group broadly rebounded from July’s technology-led pullback. The Nasdaq-100 Select Equal Weighted™ Index (NDXSE™) led with a gain of 6.4%, followed by the Nasdaq-100 Technology Sector™ Index (NDXT™ ) at 6.0%, the Nasdaq-100 High Beta Index™ (NDXHB™) at 5.9%, and the Nasdaq Innovators Completion Cap™ Index (NCX™) , also at 5.9%. The Nasdaq-100 Index® (NDX®) advanced 4.2%, extending its year-to-date return to 16.7%, while the Nasdaq-100 Equal Weighted™ Index (NDXE™) gained 4.1% and remained ahead of the cap-weighted index year to date with a 19.1% return. Overall, this group of indexes gained an average of 3.6%. Nasdaq Global Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. Performance across the Nasdaq Global Indexes suite was broadly positive as all nine indexes in the group posted gains in August amid strength across both U.S. and international equities. The Nasdaq ASPA Ex Japan™ Index (NQASPAXJP™) led with a gain of 3.8%, extending its year-to-date return to 21.7%, followed by the Nasdaq Emerging Markets™ Index (NQEM™) at 3.1%. The Nasdaq US Large Cap™ Index (NQUSL™) advanced 2.8%, while the Nasdaq Global™ Index (NQGI™) and Nasdaq DM Ex United States™ Index (NQDMXUS™) each gained 2.7%. The average return for this group of indexes was 2.5%. Nasdaq Sector-Specific Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. Two of six Nasdaq Sector-Specific Indexes posted positive returns in August. The PHLX Gold/Silver Sector™ Index (XAU™) led with a gain of 32.4%, making it the top performer across all indexes in the report and lifting its year-to-date return to 19.1%. The KBW Financial Sector Dividend Yield™ Index (KDX™) followed with a gain of 5.8%. Despite slight monthly pullbacks, the KBW Nasdaq Bank™ Index (BKX™) , KBW Regional Banking™ Index (KRX™) , and KBW Premium Yield Equity REIT™ Index (KYX™) retained year-to-date gains of 12.9%, 14.6%, and 17.6%, respectively. The group averaged a gain of 4.9% for the month. Nasdaq Thematic Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. All twenty-six Nasdaq Thematic Tech Indexes with reported performance finished August in positive territory, with cloud computing, biotechnology, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence themes leading the broad rebound. The BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud™ Index (EMCLOUD™) was the top performer at 21.8%, followed by the ISE CTA Cloud Computing™ Index (CPQ™) at 15.6% and the Nasdaq Lux Health Tech™ Index (NQHTEC™) at 12.7%. The Nasdaq Biotechnology® Index (NBI®) advanced 10.4%, lifting its year-to-date return to 24.8%. The Nasdaq CTA Cybersecurity™ Index (NQCYBR™) and Nasdaq CTA Artificial Intelligence™ Index (NQINTEL™) gained 9.0% and 7.2%, respectively, extending their year-to-date returns to 40.1% and 38.8%. The group averaged a gain of 6.6% for the month. Nasdaq Thematic Renewables & Energy Transition Materials Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. Twelve of seventeen indexes in the Nasdaq Thematic Renewables & Energy Transition Materials group posted positive returns in August, with the group averaging a gain of 11.5% as metals and mining themes strengthened. The Nasdaq Sprott Silver Miners™ Index (NSLVR™) led with a gain of 31.4%, followed by the Nasdaq Junior Silver Miners™ Index (NMFSM™) at 30.5%. The Nasdaq Sprott Energy Transition Materials™ Index (NSETM™) , Nasdaq Sprott Energy Transition Materials Select™ Index (METAL™) , and Nasdaq Sprott Junior Copper Miners™ Index (NSCOPJ™) each gained more than 20%, with year-to-date returns of 19.6%, 22.6%, and 21.0%, respectively. Nasdaq Crypto Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. All three Nasdaq Crypto Indexes finished August in positive territory as crypto assets extended their rebound from July amid renewed interest in the “debasement trade.” The rally coincided with the U.S. Treasury’s announcement of increased securities buybacks and efforts to temper rate expectations, according to Bloomberg, supporting demand for alternative stores of value and higher-beta assets. The Nasdaq Ether Settlement Price™ Index (NQETHS™) led with a gain of 33.0%, followed by the Nasdaq Crypto Settlement Price™ Index (NCIS™) at 27.0% and the Nasdaq Bitcoin Settlement Price™ Index (NQBTCS™) at 25.4%. Despite the strong monthly recovery, the indexes remained down 16.4%, 12.0%, and 9.7% year to date, respectively. The group averaged a return of 28.5% for the month. Nasdaq Quantitative Indexes Across the index suites comprising Nasdaq’s quantitative offerings, 41 out of 54 indexes posted gains in August, averaging a gain of 1.8%. Nasdaq Options & Other Quantitative Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. All ten Nasdaq Options & Other Quantitative Indexes finished August in positive territory as commodity-linked strategies and Nasdaq-100 options strategies advanced. The Credit Suisse Nasdaq Silver FLOWS106 TR™ Index (QSLVOTR™) led with a gain of 14.3%, making it the top performer, followed by the Credit Suisse Nasdaq Gold FLOWS103 TR™ Index (QGLDITR™) at 7.6% and the Credit Suisse Nasdaq WTI Crude Oil FLOWS106 TR™ Index (QUSOITR™) at 5.8%. The WTI-linked strategy extended its year-to-date return to 41.2%. Options-overwrite strategies also participated in the advance, with the CBOE Nasdaq-100 Half BuyWrite™ Index (BXNH™) and CBOE Nasdaq-100 BuyWrite™ Index (BXNT™) each gaining 4.2%. The group averaged a gain of 4.9% for the month. Nasdaq Multifactor Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. Eleven of thirteen Nasdaq Multifactor Indexes finished August in positive territory, averaging a gain of 0.8% for the month as growth, value, and international momentum exposures contributed to performance. The Growth Strength™ Index (NQCAPSG™) led with a gain of 2.4%, followed by the Nasdaq Victory International Value Momentum™ Index (VMILMN™) and Capital Strength™ Index (NQCAPST™) , which each gained 1.8%. The international value-momentum strategy extended its year-to-date return to 23.1%, while the Nasdaq AlphaDEX Large Cap Value™ Index (NQDXUSLCV™) advanced 1.4% and remained up 18.5% year to date. Nasdaq Dorsey Wright Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. Nine of sixteen Nasdaq Dorsey Wright Indexes finished August in positive territory with emerging markets and energy strategies leading the suite. The Dorsey Wright Emerging Markets Tech Leaders™ Index (DWAEM™) led with a gain of 12.3%, lifting its year-to-date return to 41.4%, while the Dorsey Wright Energy Tech Leaders™ Index (DWEN™) gained 7.8% and remained up 41.8% year to date. The Dorsey Wright Focus Five™ Index (DWANQFF™) rose 5.6%, extending its year-to-date return to 16.8%, while the Dorsey Wright Healthcare Tech Leaders™ Index (DWHC™) added 4.6% and reached a year-to-date return of 22.6%. The group averaged a 1.5% gain for the month. Nasdaq Dividend & Income Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. Eleven of fifteen Nasdaq Dividend & Income Indexes finished August in positive territory, with the group averaging a gain of 0.8% as technology-dividend, buyback, and high-equity-income strategies led. title: From "Export" to "Overseas Revenue": A Share Evidence of China’s Global Expansion
author: Phoebe Wang
description: China’s corporate globalization story has entered a new phase. Exports still matter, but they no longer capture the full picture. As companies expand overseas sales networks and operations, overseas revenue provides a more direct signal of globalization than exports alone.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways China’s globalization is evolving beyond exports. Overseas revenue is becoming a more meaningful indicator of global expansion as Chinese companies build international sales networks and operations, rather than relying solely on exports. Global exposure remains uneven but meaningful. While many companies still have limited international revenue, a growing segment has substantial overseas exposure Companies with higher overseas revenue tend to outperform. Technology companies show the deepest international penetration. A significant portion of overseas revenue in the IT sector comes from firms where international markets account for more than half of total revenue. China’s corporate globalization story has entered a new phase. Exports still matter, but they no longer capture the full picture. As companies expand overseas sales networks and operations, overseas revenue provides a more direct signal of globalization than exports alone. Using A-share disclosures  , this blog documents how overseas revenue has broadened across the onshore universe, become more material in aggregate, and diverged meaningfully across industries. While the theme also spans offshore listings, the analysis here focuses on A-shares to quantify how overseas revenue exposure has evolved within the onshore listed universe. Overseas Revenue Expansion Is Broadening and Becoming More Material The “going global” narrative is sometimes framed as a story driven by a small set of exporters. A-share disclosures suggest something broader. More companies are reporting non-zero overseas revenue in annual reports, indicating that overseas revenue exposure is becoming increasingly common across the listed universe. Chart 1 puts that growth in context by showing both the total A-share universe and the subset reporting overseas revenue. From 2015 to 2025, the total coun t rose from 2,808 to 5,470, while companies reporting overseas revenue increased from 1,615 to 3,803, lifting the share from roughly 58% to nearly 70%. This points to overseas revenue becoming a more standard feature of A-share disclosure over time. Chart 1: Number of Globalization Participants Breadth, however, is only part of the picture. The more important question is whether overseas revenue is becoming economically meaningful in aggregate. The revenue mix data ( Chart 2 ) points to a sustained growth differential: over 2015–2025, overseas revenue grew at a +15.17% 10-year CAGR, compared with +8.68% for domestic revenue. That gap has gradually lifted overseas revenue’s share of total revenue from 10% in 2015 to 17% in 2025. The overseas share slipped from 13% in 2019 to 12% in 2020 and remained at 12% in 2021, a pattern that is consistent with the pandemic-era disruption to cross-border demand and logistics. From 2022 onward, overseas revenue resumed its upward trajectory, while domestic revenue has moderated in the most recent years. Chart 2: A-share Companies' Overseas Revenue Grew Faster than Domestic Revenue Aggregate trends can still mask how uneven overseas exposure is across individual companies. A distribution view helps distinguish companies with incidental overseas revenue from those for which overseas markets are central to the business. Chart 3 shows that overseas revenue exposure remains skewed toward the lower end: 2,426 companies fall in the 0%–25% overseas revenue share bucket. Another 1,667 companies report zero overseas revenue. At the other end, a meaningful subset has built deeper overseas footprints, with 755 companies in the 25%–50% bucket and 622 companies with more than 50% of revenue from overseas. Median market capitalization is relatively similar across buckets, clustered in the 6–7 billion CNY range, suggesting the dispersion is not primarily a size effect. Chart 3: Overseas Revenue Share Bucket With breadth, the shift in the revenue mix toward overseas revenue, and the dispersion established, it is natural to ask whether companies with overseas revenue exposure also look different on fundamentals. Overseas Revenue Exposure Aligns with Stronger Growth and Quality Metrics In this section, the data is kept intentionally straightforward. Companies are grouped by overseas revenue share as of year-end 2025, and the comparison focuses on one growth metric, one profitability metric, and one earnings-growth metric. Chart 4a shows a separation between purely domestic companies and those with overseas revenue exposure. Median three-year annualized sales growth is measured over FY2022 to FY2025. Recent sales growth is essentially flat for the zero overseas revenue bucket at 0.14%, then steps higher once overseas revenue appears and continues to rise with greater overseas exposure, reaching 6.25% in the more than 50% bucket. Chart 4a: Sales Growth by Overseas Revenue Share Bucket Profitability shows a similar gradient ( Chart 4b ). Median Return on Equity (ROE) rises from 2.79% in the zero-overseas bucket to 6.61% in the more than 50% bucket. ROE is a simple gauge of how much profit a company generates for each unit of shareholder equity and the upward profile suggests that higher overseas exposure is associated with stronger capital efficiency in this year-end 2025 snapshot. Chart 4b: ROE by Overseas Revenue Share Bucket Chart 4c adds an earnings momentum lens. Median profit growth over FY2022 to FY2025 is negative through the lower and middle buckets, but turns positive at 3.58% in the more than 50% bucket. Read alongside Charts 4a and 4b , the profit-growth distribution suggests that the strongest overseas-exposure cohort is also where earnings growth has been more resilient in recent years. Chart 4c: Profit Growth by Overseas Revenue Share Bucket The year-end 2025 bucket view links deeper overseas exposure with stronger growth, profitability, and earnings momentum. With median outcomes calculated across sizeable buckets and median market caps clustered in a relatively narrow band across buckets ( Chart 3 ), the pattern is unlikely to be driven by a small number of extreme observations or a simple size effect. Overseas Revenue Concentrates in China’s Advantage Industries As overseas revenue becomes more visible in A-shares, two questions matter most: which sectors contribute the bulk of overseas revenue, and where overseas revenue is deepest at the company level. Overseas revenue is not evenly distributed across A-shares; it clusters in sectors where China’s global competitiveness is most visible. Chart 5 makes that concentration intuitive by comparing each sector’s share of total revenue with its share of total overseas revenue. Industrials remains the anchor because it is large in the domestic economy and stays large overseas. The sharper signal is the overweight in Information Technology and Consumer Discretionary: both are 9% of total revenue, yet they account for 19% and 17% of overseas revenue, respectively. This is consistent with the broader narrative of China’s evolving advantage—from pure shipping-volume exports to competitiveness in electronics, digital-enabling hardware, and scalable consumer products and channels, areas where global trade and supply chains have increasingly centered in Asia and where China has deepened its manufacturing and export presence. Financials remains predominantly domestic-facing, representing 13% of total revenue but only a minimal share of overseas revenue. Chart 5: Industry Contribution to Total Revenue vs. Total Overseas Revenue The depth view ( Chart 6 ) separates broad participation from global-first profiles by splitting sector overseas revenue across exposure buckets. Industrials leads in absolute overseas revenue, with contributions spread across buckets, consistent with broad participation at varying overseas intensity. Information Technology shows greater depth, with a meaningful share coming from the more than 50% bucket, indicating overseas markets are central for a sizeable subset of A-share tech names. Consumer Discretionary tilts toward 25%–50%. Materials is more bifurcated, with weight in both 0%–25% and more than 50%. Energy leans heavily toward 25%–50%, consistent with overseas revenue becoming material as globalization scales, even if it is not yet the primary revenue source. Chart 6: Globalization “Depth” by Industry Overall, the year-end 2025 sector view shows Industrials leading in absolute overseas revenue, with deeper globalization most evident in Information Technology and a scaling profile more common in sectors such as Energy. Conclusion Across A-shares, overseas revenue has become more prevalent, more material in the aggregate mix, and more concentrated in sectors where China tends to compete globally. In future blog posts, we will build on these findings and examine how overseas revenue exposure can be framed as an investment theme and why investors may care. title: Nasdaq Advances Always-On Markets and Tokenized Equities Strategy with Agreement to Invest in Payward
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: Nasdaq announced it has agreed to invest in Payward, the parent company of leading global crypto platform Kraken. This collaboration centers on infrastructure supporting tokenized equities, always-on markets, and the convergence of financial systems and decentralized networks.
content: Nasdaq is taking the next step toward a more connected financial system, advancing the infrastructure needed to support the movement of capital, assets, and liquidity across markets. The company announced today that it has agreed to invest $100 million in Payward, the parent company of leading global crypto platform Kraken. This agreement to invest from Nasdaq Ventures will significantly deepen a relationship first announced in March, when Nasdaq announced its plans to launch an equity token design in coordination with Payward that will put public companies at the center of ownership rights, transparency, and governance. Nasdaq Ventures’ agreement to invest in Payward reflects Nasdaq's conviction in Payward's long-term potential and its role in supporting market modernization, further aligning the two companies as they collaborate on infrastructure supporting tokenized equities, always-on markets, and the convergence of financial systems and decentralized networks. "The next era of market evolution will be defined by how efficiently and seamlessly capital and assets move across the financial system with durable, high-integrity liquidity," said Tal Cohen, President, Nasdaq. "Expanding our relationship with Payward reflects our conviction that Kraken can play an important role in building the infrastructure that supports this evolution. Our partnership advances our work on Nasdaq Equity Tokens and helps build a more connected financial system while preserving the trust, transparency and integrity that underpin capital formation." The agreement to invest in Payward follows the August launch of Nasdaq’s Digital Liquidity Networks (DLN) markets business , which aims to bring together liquidity platforms, tokenization capabilities, and fintech solutions serving the digital assets ecosystem. Together, Payward brings Kraken’s crypto-native execution venue and the xStocks infrastructure layer, and Nasdaq contributes wide-ranging expertise, regulated market infrastructure, surveillance technologies, and more. In addition to the ongoing partnership on tokenized equities, the companies announced today that Payward will adopt Nasdaq's market-leading market surveillance technology, to ensure integrity across Payward's full portfolio of trading venues. Driving the Future of Tokenized Equities As boundaries between mainstream and digital markets are converging, and demand for always-on, programmable liquidity is accelerating, Nasdaq is building the infrastructure that will define and enable this convergence. Following this new investment, Nasdaq and Payward will continue to advance their work on building the operational and commercial infrastructure to support the proposed Nasdaq Equity Tokens (NETs) design by connecting it with Payward's xStocks ecosystem. Nasdaq expects to launch NETs in the second quarter of 2027. That work has already established a foundation for how tokenized equities could move across different market environments while maintaining their intended form for the benefit of issuers and investors. Now, the next phase of the collaboration is focused on advancing the distribution, settlement and trading capabilities needed to support broader adoption of tokenized equities, including interoperability between NETs and Payward's xStocks ecosystem CAUTIONARY NOTE REGARDING FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS Information set forth in this communication contains forward-looking statements that involve a number of risks and uncertainties. title: LBMA Precious Metals market volumes, June-August 2026, and their significance
author: StoneX
description: Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery.  Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Precious metals experienced three distinct phases during June-August 2026: early weakness, summer consolidation, and a strong recovery in August. Silver remained the strongest performer, gaining approximately 159% over the previous year. ETF holdings increased and speculative long positions expanded significantly during August, reflecting renewed investor confidence. Options volumes nearly doubled compared to the same period in 2025, highlighting increased hedging and speculative activity. The LBMA precious metals market between June and August 2026 was defined by a transition from correction to recovery. Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery. Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain Rhona O’Connell, StoneX Financial Ltd; 4 th September May 2026 Any views expressed here are of the writer and do not reflect a house view from NASDAQ. Welcome to our monthly round-up of the LBMA OTC trading volumes in gold, silver, platinum and palladium, as recorded on a daily basis by the Association. These are split into spot, swap/forward, options and LoanLeaseDeposit (LLD) and give a flavour of the markets’ activity and how they were influenced by external forces and news items.   Due to technical issues plus some holiday leave, this piece looks back at the June-August this year against June-August 2025 All references to COMEX or NYMEX positioning refer to Managed Money, not commercial positions. General introduction: Daily June-August average compared with daily average for the equivalent period in 2025. Source: LBMA Source: LBMA, StoneX Colour coding ranks the metals against each other in each sector June to August was a particularly eventful period for the precious complex, with the intersection of a hawkish new Fed, an interventionist Treasury, a re-escalating Gulf war, and a structurally weak dollar. Gold, silver, platinum and palladium, September 2025 to early September 2026 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver still the outperformer at +159%; Platinum 125%, Gold 124% and palladium, 118% The three key drivers overall included the vicissitudes of the Gulf war, a dollar that was weak against the euro while strong against the yen – although it could be argued that the yen was independently weak - and a virtual tug-of-war developed between Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen, which is particularly relevant for gold. By the end of the period, the dollar-debasement argument, which had been fading, reasserted itself. After the rally in May, especially in silver, all four metals drifted lower through June and July as the summer doldrums set in and once again some major players were unwilling to take strategic positions.  The dollar strengthened in June during the ceasefire in the Gulf but once escalation had resumed the currency entered a downward path that only paused for breath in late August. The metals did rally in late June as the Gulf ceasefire failed, with reciprocal strikes between the US and Iran raising new doubts over the return of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.  As we write in early September those doubts have still not been dispelled. In the background it was interesting to see the rising correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield, but not that surprising since they are both rooted around the Gulf conflict and by definition gold forms part of this matrix also. Growing correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield since the onset of hostilities Source: Bloomberg, StoneX January 2025 – early September2026 spot volumes, tonnes Gold Silver Source: for all charts above; LBMA, StoneX Platinum Palladium COMEX, NYMEX, positioning to 25 th August 2026 GOLD SILVER PLATINUM PALLADIUM Source: CFTC, StoneX Gold Gold sold off hard in June then spent July trading around $4,100 and occasionally dipping toward $4,000 in one interesting development, gold opened lower on July 13 and fell further despite the US–Iran airstrikes over that weekend, a telling sign that the hawkish-Fed/yield story was overriding the geopolitical safe-haven bid at that point. From a mid-July trough just below$4,000, the metal then staged its best stretch of the year, rallying: by 18% from its mid-July low to an intraday high of $4,696 on August 25 th , its highest since mid-May, before snapping a five-day winning streak late in the month after US inflation data came in above target, then steadying near $4,400–$4,600 into month-end. That mid-August week was gold's best since January, and gold-mining stocks had their hottest five-day run since 2008. Inverted gold and the real two-year yield Source: Bloomberg, StoneX It may seem counter-intuitive that gold prices were rising in the face of continuing increases in bond yields, but this is explained as follows.  Yields were rising on inflation and fiscal fears  rather than growth; a widening fiscal deficit, inflation persistently above 2% (for 65 months above target as Keviin Warsh noted in his Jackson Hole presentation at end-August), a weaker dollar, and an avalanche of corporate bond issuance to fund AI and data-centre build-outs — which is precisely an environment in which gold can flourish. Second, and probably more significantly, the Treasury Secretary’s efforts to suppress yields via FX intervention (something which almost invariably fails) were seen by the markets as an effort at fiscal dominance and financial repression: an admission that the debt load could no longer tolerate market-clearing rates. Sure enough, by early September 30-year yields were back over 5.2%. The US 5Y-30Y curve; long-term Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Adding to gold’s August rally were soft inflation numbers, but not soft enough for the Fed and Mr Warsh’s Jackson Hole comments were visibly more hawkish than the post-FOMC Press conferences held previously. Trading activity Turnover, M ounces Source: NASDAQ, LBMA As far as market turnover is concerned, the sell-off in early June was in the heaviest volume of the period, with over 30M ounces traded on each of three consecutive days.  The rest of June was relatively busy but turnover in July was paltry.  After some improvement in early August, the 5 th was particularly heavy as optimism grew over the possibility of Hormuz being reopened and with hedge funds getting on board gold rallied from $4,066 to $4,268, laying the foundations for consolidation in a new range, and latterly for the rally to almost $4,700 at month-end.  That rally was in relatively thin conditions until the high-volume sell-off on the 28 th in the wake of Kevin Warsh’s comments. Gold from September 2025 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Among the OTC derivative sectors, swaps/forwards were sluggish in June until towards month-end when, after falling below the 10-day moving average, forward activity picked up and helped to drive the price to the low for the period ($3,943 intraday). Activity increased in July and on more than one occasion seemed to be related to technical indicators, notably the moving averages. This was mirrored to an extent in the LLD segment, notably in early mid-July where heavy activity around $4,100 suggests that there was some supply-side hedging going through the market as prices failed at this level.  As LLD volumes drifted off, the path higher became easier and indeed there was only one LLD trading day in August and that came on the 5th, quelling an initial attempt to clear $4,400. Volumes were high in mid-late July, with prices moving sideways, suggesting good two-way activity.  After a busy day early in August, with a failed assault on $4,400, swaps/forwards tailed off. Finally the options market the volume over the period was almost double that of June-August 2025, with a daily average of almost 1.1M ounces. Even so, volumes were sluggish in June and July.  The stand-out day, with 4.9M ounces going through was again 5 th August, along with high volumes in spot and swaps/forwards, suggesting that part of that swollen volume was hedging against options exposure.  This was on that same day when the market rallied off the 20-day moving average at $4065 to $4,268; i.e. the 5 th when on hopes that Hormuz would reopen. Over the period the ETF gold holdings opened at 4,121t, briefly continued the decline that had started in mid-May, but then turned higher to close Augst at 4,181t, a net year-to-date gain of 156t.  CFTC figures show outright Managed money longs rising from 402t to 497t on 25 th August, while outright shorts fluctuated from 54t to 64t the following week, fluctuated around 50t for much of the rest of the period before short covering into 23t in early Augst ; they closed the period higher again, at 47t. Gold and the S&P (log-scales) Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver As usual, silver was the highest-beta play on the same macro forces outlined above, and once again it moved violently. After a January record near $121–$122, it had already halved by early summer, opening June at $74 before a two-leg tumble to $56 on the 24 th , and entering a five-week period in a sideways trend between$55 and $63. This set the scene for the August recovery, with silver reaching an intraday high of &1 on the 28 th before, with gold, going into reverse post-Warsh. Gold and silver action, correlation Source: Bloomberg As well as the major factors that drove gold and by association, silver, the latter metal also has its industrial character to address, given that 70% of silver fabrication (ex-investment) is in industrial uses.  The June-quarter hawkish Fed hold at 3.50–3.75% and a divided committee hit silver's industrial engine directly, and the gold-silver ratio widened from a May low near 55:1 to about 69:1 by mid-July — a classic sign of silver underperforming gold in a risk-off environment. The same soft-data/weak-dollar cocktail that lifted gold then drove the August rebound, amplified by silver's leverage.  The August rally was accompanied, and to some extent driven by, the return of Managed Monay longs (after quite an exodus earlier in the year), rising from 2,822t in mid-July to 3,444t in late August, while shorts were slower to respond, having continued to expand to 1,368t in  mid-August (from 941t in mid-July) then contracting to 1,143t in late August. Gold:silver ratio Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Although the US economy is relatively resilient and the onset of AI, vehicle electrification and solar cells will combine to take silver into an expanding pre-investment deficit, in the immediate term these forces are muffled to a degree with the current surplus of solar cells (and a minor threat from copper) while the ebbs and flows of vehicle electrification are a matter of record – although this is more relevant to the PGM than to silver; see below. Turnover Source:  NASDAQ Spot volumes were down 39% over the period compared with June-August 2025.  With the exception of 5 th August, much mentioned in our gold comments (Hormuz hopes), silver’s spot volume fluctuations were similar to those of gold with high volume in the June retreat (thus making the market less crowded) and then a sluggish period through to mid-July. As prices stabilised spot activity cautiously increased, although volumes in the rally to $70, which was reached on 21 st August, were patchy.  On the 21 st , volumes were much livelier. As hedging activity developed (increased volumes in swaps/forwards and options also) and called a halt to the rally.  After three successive efforts to clear $70, the market capitulated and the sharp fall to $66 on the 28 th was in heavy spot volume (but not in the derivatives). Derivatives activity was heavy in June in swaps and forwards, which will certainly have been instrumental in the price fall and would to some extent have been self-fulfilling.  The LLD segment was 25% down on the 2025 equivalent and here, too , was busiest in the June fall.  There was some cautious interest in mid-August when silver was flirting with $65, suggesting some hedging, especially as the price didn’t clear that level at that stage.  Finally there was activity at month-end as silver was again on the retreat. Platinum and palladium Platinum was the "cleanest" fundamental story of the four, driven more by physical scarcity than by the dollar. The market is expected to be in deficit for the fourth consecutive year this year, despite expected falls in auto and jewellery demand, while supply is likely to be broadly steady.  South Africa accounts for roughly 72% of refined production, and that concentration was the summer's active risk. National primary output fell from about 5.3 million ounces in 2006 to roughly 3.9 million in 2025 and while looking steady this year it is expected to decline again next year. On the demand side, the hydrogen fuel-cell demand, while coming from a very low base, adds a new industrial floor. Palladium trades heavily on autos (80% of demand comes from catalytic converters in gasoline and hybrid vehicles) so it is exposed to two secular headwinds; platinum substitution and the rise of battery-electric vehicles. The June price softness reflected slower automaker procurement, soft electronics demand, caution in the jewellery sector, plus almost non-existent investment, while supply was steady. The July bounce was seasonal restocking rather than scarcity.  The one genuine supply-side tail risk remains geopolitical — Russia is the world's largest palladium producer (nickel by-product), followed by South Africa (platinum by-product) so any escalation of sanctions on Russian metal would be the scenario that could override the surplus narrative, much as it did in 2022.  This is still up in the air. Turnover Source: NASDAQ Platinum spot turnover was 49% down on the equivalent period of 2025, while options and LLD were both down by ~20%.  Swaps/forwards were the only sector in the black, up by 21%.  Trading volumes were choppy, with a couple of heavy days trading in spot in the first week as prices came extended a slide from $1,980 ,although this was not mirrored in the OTC derivatives. The sharp fall from $1,906 to $1,772 was one of those days, and Spot volumes dwindled thereafter as prices slid to $1,535 on 1st July. At this point spot and forwards kicked in, in a classic surge in volume in a price reversal and   suggesting industrial forward buying, sparking a period of price consolidation, during which the only point of interest was heavy forward activity on the approach to $1,700, which failed, implying continued industrial interest and quite possibly inventory management. Early August saw heavy volumes in spot forwards and options as prices surged from $1,629 to$1,751, stemming from a second day of oil price declines and a weaker dollar (Gulf again), taking all the metals higher and precipitating a change of range.  After a period of consolidation the rally to a four-time failed test of $1,900 enjoyed good volumes in everything except options and the reversal saw strong spot activity, suggesting profit taking / stale bull liquidation. Platinum, palladium and the ratio, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Palladium prices moved closely in line with platinum over the period, with the correlation between the two not dropping below 0.84, and reaching 0.90 on occasion. Spot trading patterns were not that similar, however, with the early June fall being more of a thin volume slide. There was some intermittent interest in late July in both spot and forwards as the market started to benefit from its prior period of price consolidation, and setting the scene for the sharp jump in early August that had affected all four metals.  Forwards were busy in late July on the approach to $1,300, while there was little options activity until mid-August as prices completed a bear move from the failure at $1,400.   That failure had itself been accompanied by heavy LLD volume, suggesting some hedging activity. Platinum, palladium and the spread, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX

title: The Value of Data Becomes Even More Important in an AI-Powered Financial System
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: Nasdaq's latest whitepaper, Unlocking Financial Markets: Understanding the Role of Data in a Digital Economy, examines how data powers modern capital markets and why trusted information has become one of the most important forms of financial infrastructure.
content: The financial industry is entering another period of profound transformation. The first major shift moved markets from crowded trading floors to electronic infrastructure. The next is already underway. Artificial intelligence is reshaping how decisions are made. Trading is becoming increasingly automated. Market participants are preparing for always-on markets, faster settlement cycles, and new forms of digital infrastructure. Together, these developments point toward a future that is faster, more interconnected, and increasingly dependent on data. That reality sits at the center of Nasdaq's latest whitepaper, Unlocking Financial Markets: Understanding the Role of Data in a Digital Economy , which examines how data powers modern capital markets and why trusted information has become one of the most important forms of financial infrastructure. While conversations about financial data often focus on cost, the paper argues that a more important question is value. "Data is the foundation of every modern financial decision," said Brandon Tepper, Senior Vice President and Global Head of Data for Nasdaq's Capital Access Platforms. "As markets become more automated and AI-enabled, the quality and integrity of the data underneath those decisions becomes increasingly important." Building the Financial Data Stack The financial ecosystem relies on a broad range of information sources. At the base is exchange market data, which provides a transparent view of regulated market activity and serves as the foundation for price discovery. Above that layer sits a growing ecosystem of complementary and alternative data products, including indices, analytics, research, news, and other datasets that help firms generate additional insight. This layered structure has expanded dramatically over the past decade as firms seek new ways to analyze markets, manage risk, and uncover opportunities. Global spending on financial market data surpassed $50 billion in 2025, reflecting growing demand for increasingly sophisticated datasets and analytical tools. Yet the paper finds that the value created throughout the broader ecosystem ultimately depends on the quality and integrity of the foundational layer beneath it. Exchange data serves as the common reference point against which other datasets, analytics, and models are built and validated. A useful way to think about the relationship is through infrastructure. New applications, analytics tools, and AI models may represent the visible innovations attracting attention across the industry, but they depend on an underlying foundation that must remain reliable, resilient, and universally trusted. Why AI Raises the Stakes The growing adoption of artificial intelligence is amplifying the importance of high-quality financial data. AI systems can identify patterns, generate predictions, and automate decisions, but they do not independently determine what is true. Their outputs are only as reliable as the data on which they are trained, tested, and governed. As a result, trusted exchange market data plays a critical role as both a training and validation layer for AI-enabled finance. Standardized, transparent, and auditable market information helps ensure that models remain anchored to observable market outcomes rather than incomplete, fragmented, or unverified signals. This becomes increasingly important as firms deploy AI across portfolio management, trading, risk management, surveillance, compliance, and investment research. In more automated environments, errors can be propagated at greater speed and scale, increasing the importance of maintaining trusted sources of market truth. The paper argues that AI is not reducing the importance of exchange data. Instead, it is increasing demand for the trusted reference layer that allows firms to evaluate models, measure performance, and manage risk with confidence. Preparing for an Always-On Future Artificial intelligence is only one part of a broader evolution underway across financial markets. Industry initiatives ranging from extended trading hours and accelerated settlement to the growing use of digital assets and on-chain infrastructure are creating a financial system that operates with greater speed and continuity than ever before. In that environment, trusted data becomes even more essential. Risk systems require accurate information. Automated workflows require reliable inputs. Smart contracts and digital infrastructure still depend on trusted reference prices that connect automated actions to real-world market value. As the financial system becomes more interconnected, the importance of maintaining a transparent, standardized, and continuously available foundation of market data only grows. "The future financial system will undoubtedly introduce new technologies and new capabilities," Tepper said. "But innovation doesn't eliminate the need for trusted information. If anything, it increases the importance of having a shared source of truth that market participants can rely on." The Foundation of Future Innovation Innovation across financial services continues to accelerate. New data products, analytics platforms, AI workflows, and investment tools are creating significant value throughout the industry. But the research suggests that the success of those innovations remains closely linked to the integrity of the underlying market information from which they derive value. title: What is Driving Free Cash Flow Yield Performance in Japan?
author: Johnny Chen
description: Free cash flow is the cash a company has left after paying for its operations and investments. Free cash flow ETFs first appeared in the United States in 2016 and began expanding into the APAC region in 2023. This study examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns. Because free cash flow yield puts price in the denominator, high free cash flow yield is easily linked to low valuation. The free cash flow component (FCF/B) has demonstrated a steady upward trend over the period from May 2007 through June 2026 Beyond answering the value question, this points to a further possibility worth exploring: FCF/B on its own may be a viable building block for a free cash flow strategy in Japan. Free cash flow is the cash a company has left after paying for its operations and investments. Free cash flow ETFs first appeared in the United States in 2016 and began expanding into the APAC region in 2023. This study examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns. The Rise of Free Cash Flow Strategies in APAC The free cash flow strategy gained significant momentum in APAC recently, with total 35 free cash flow ETFs have been launched in China, Hong Kong, Japan and Korea between 1 January 2023 and 30 June 2026. Chart 1 shows that two newly listed free cash flow ETFs in Japan, each with more than one year of performance history, Global X MSCI Japan Cash Flow Kings ETF 234A and Global X S&P 500 Cash Flow Top 100 ETF (356A) , have delivered one-year total returns of 40% and 33%, as of 30 June 2026. Chart 1: The Launch Trend of Free Cash Flow ETFs Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Product Intelligence Japan Cash Flow ETF 234A invests in the universe of top 500 large and mid-cap Japanese stocks and is constructed by selecting the 50 stocks with the highest free cash flow yield from the universe. We are interested in whether this free cash flow yield strategy can deliver long-term outperformance and what drives its returns. Examining Long-Term Historical Performance and Value Exposure ETF 234A is a newly launched product with limited history, so we use its underlying index of this ETF to represent the long-term performance of free cash flow yield in Japan. TOPIX 500 index is used as market benchmark because the underlying index is also using the top 500 large and mid-cap as universe. Chart 2 shows that since May 2007, the underlying index of this ETF has delivered an annualized total return of 8.6%, while TOPIX 500 has delivered only 2.6%. This suggests that free cash flow yield in Japan not only generated strong one-year performance (40%) but also outperformed the benchmark from 31 May 2007 to 30 June 2026. The price denominator in free cash flow yield (free cash flow per share divided by stock price) from ETF 234A shares the same denominator as value factor (book value divided by stock price) of TOPIX 500 value index. The TOPIX 500 value index has surged since 2023 following the launch of Japan value program which is a Tokyo stock exchange initiative that encourages Japanese companies, particularly those with low share prices relative to their assets to use capital more efficiently, improve profitability, and better reward shareholders. Compared with the TOPIX 500 value Index, the underlying index of ETF 234A has exhibited a similar surge in returns since 2023, as shown in Chart 2. Therefore, we would like to determine whether the returns based on free cash flow yield are driven by the value factor. Chart 2: Japan Cash Flow Kings ETF 234A Index Performance vs Benchmarks Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Index Research & Development Looking Inside Free Cash Flow Yield 1) A Factor Lens: Value Matters, so Do Quality and Investment Factors We applied Fama-French five factor model, which is a model that explains asset returns using multiple risk factors rather than just the market, on the underlying index of ETF 234A and TOPIX 500. The model result shown in Chart 3 indicates a higher coefficient and statistically significant exposure to the value factor whereas TOPIX 500’s exposure to value is limited. In 2025, the value factor was associated with the underlying index of ETF 234A 1-year 30% return by adding 7.6 points, which is about 25% of the total return. Overall, the model suggests that the underlying index combines large-cap, value with additional tilts toward companies earning strong profits (high quality) and conservative investing. Chart 3: Output of Fama-French 5 Factor Model Source: Fama-French Model, Nasdaq Index Research & Development 2) Separating Cash-Flow Strength from Valuation for Regression Decomposition Given that free cash flow yield uses stock price in the denominator, a natural question is whether high free cash flow yield companies largely overlap with low-valuation names, and therefore exhibit high exposure to the value factor. More importantly, to what extent is the observed performance of the “free cash flow yield” explained by this value exposure? To address this question, we decompose free cash flow yield by expressing it as Free Cash Flow Per Share / Price = Free Cash Flow Per Share / Book Value (free cash flow component)  × Book Value / Price (value component). We then applied the return decomposition framework below to regress the daily returns of the high free cash flow yield portfolio on the TOPIX 500 market return, the free cash flow‑to‑book value return premium, and the book value-to-price premium. This approach allows us to separate the return contributions from the overall market, the free cash flow component, and the value component. Note: The high free cash flow yield portfolio on the left hand side was constructed by selecting the top 250 high free cash flow yield stocks from the top 500 large‑ and mid‑cap universe in Japan. The return premium on the right hand side were constructed using the same methodology as the high free cash flow yield portfolio. The regression results indicate that the high free cash flow yield portfolio’s returns may be driven by market, while both free cash flow‑to‑book value and book value-to-price provide additional independent explanatory power with t-stat 9.57 and 8.93 respectively. Both the free cash flow‑to‑book value and book value-to-price premiums are statistically significant (at the 1% level), not just one. This shows that the free cash flow‑to‑book value component contributes to returns independently of value, beyond the shared price denominator. 3) Interaction Between Free Cash Flow-to-Book and Value Component After showing that both free cash flow‑to‑book value and book‑to‑price are important in explaining returns, the next step is to see whether they interact with each other. In other words, do companies with high free cash flow‑to‑book value behave like traditional value stocks (high book value‑to‑price), or are they different? Looking at the TOPIX 500, if we divide the 500 stocks into high and low groups based on their free cash flow component and value component separately, only one-third of the high free cash flow-to-book stocks also belong to high value group, which indicates that free cash flow and value are capturing different names from the universe. Chart 4 shows the backtested relative performance of each metric, constructed as the high-metric group index divided by the low-metric group. The free cash flow yield (Top 500 FCF/P) tracks the free cash flow component (Top 500 FCF/B) closely, both delivering steady gains. The value component (Top 500 B/P) follows a different path. It led from 2021 to early 2026 but gave back much of that gain over the past four months and saw larger drawdowns throughout. In short, free cash flow yield behaves more like the free cash flow component than like value. Chart 4: Free Cash Flow‑to‑Book Value and Book Value-to-Price Return Premium Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Index Research & Development Conclusion Because free cash flow yield puts price in the denominator, high free cash flow yield is easily linked to low valuation. But our factor attribution and regression analysis show the free cash flow component has explanatory power beyond value. Furthermore, when decomposing free cash flow yield into its free cash flow and value components, we found that not only is the constituent overlap between the high free cash flow component group and the value group relatively low, but the two groups have also exhibited distinct return patterns. Compared with the existing free cash flow yield methodology used by ETF 234A, the free cash flow component (FCF/B) has demonstrated a steady upward trend over the period from May 2007 through June 2026. Beyond answering the value question, this points to a further possibility worth exploring: FCF/B on its own may be a viable building block for a free cash flow strategy in Japan. title: Chartstopper: September 4, 2026
author: Michael Normyle
description: The two big themes this week were the rate path for the Federal Reserve and the Iran conflict.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Fed rate path in focus as Waller signals patience August jobs report blows past expectations, lifting hike odds Iran conflict pushes oil back above $90 AVGO caps a blockbuster earnings season Markets finish flat as inflation concerns offset strong earnings This Week The two big themes this week were the rate path for the Federal Reserve and the Iran conflict. For the Fed, there were two notable developments: Fed Governor Chris Waller said he was open to leaving rates unchanged if recent disinflation continues, or, as he put it, “to paraphrase John Lennon… give disinflation a chance.” The economy added 162,000 jobs in August, supporting Chair Kevin Warsh’s view last Friday that inflation is the Fed’s focus . That job gain was nearly triple expectations for 55,000 jobs added, and the previous two months were revised up, flipping July’s job change into positive territory. So, in the last week, market expectations for Fed hikes this year have increased to nearly 40 basis points (bp) from under 30bp. Of course, the Iran conflict isn’t doing the Fed any favors on the inflation front. In the last week, U.S. oil prices are up over $5 to move back above $90 per barrel – near three-month highs. That’s because hopes for any kind of near-term ceasefire seem increasingly remote after the U.S. and Iran continued to exchange strikes and more oil tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz. There were also reports that the Trump administration would not accept a return to the expired Memorandum of Understanding and would require an agreement covering both the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program. Elsewhere, second-quarter earnings season wrapped up with mega-cap AVGO beating earnings estimates with nearly 100% per annum (p.a.) growth, helping the Nasdaq-100® finish the quarter with almost 80% p.a. earnings growth. Despite the (very) strong earnings growth, concerns about inflation and rate hikes weighed on markets with the Nasdaq-100® finishing the week flat, while 10-year Treasury yields are up about 5bp to 4.8%.
